messages.body_plain:
reminder: Quantifying What it Would Take to Change an Inference: Toward a Pragmatic Sociology

Session 3476. Section on Methodology. Duncan Lecture Philadelphia Marriott Downtown, Franklin Hall 12, Level 4, 2:30-3:30pm, August 13
Kenneth Frank, Michigan State University
Host: Jim Moody

Abstract:
I quantify the conditions necessary to invalidate a statistical inference. This generates statements such as “PPP % of the estimated effect would have to be due to bias to invalidate the inference of an effect of X on Y.” Or, “An omitted variable would have to be correlated at xxx with the treatment and the outcome to invalidate an inference about the effect of X on Y.” The statements are in terms of the emphasis on unobserved quantities – robustness analysis concerns quantifying the discourse about an inference made from the best data and models already available.  I review the history and importance of sensitivity/robustness analysis in the social sciences, beginning with Cornfield’s work on smoking and lung cancer. I then present techniques for quantifying the sensitivity which are accessible in terms of conventional statistical approaches and user interface (http://konfound-it.com, STATA and R packages). Participants will leave knowing how to conduct such an analysis on an app or in a statistics package.  I conclude with new directions and potential.  Throughout I emphasize the contributions of sociologists relative to other social sciences as well as the potential of robustness analysis for the pragmatic sociologist.
